engine.title: The multibagger screen qualified nobody for four weeks
engine.body: Corrects what this entry said on 2026-08-27. It read ‘the scan is running on schedule’ and blamed the fixed list on cadence. The ledger says otherwise: the last multibagger row is 2026-08-01, while magic, magicmagic and ai_longterm — the same Saturday job, the same slot — all logged 2026-08-22. Twenty-six days, three Saturdays, nothing written.
engine.note: The screen is not broken. Run on 2026-08-27 it took 11 candidates and rejected 10 for R:R below 2.0 — CHENNPETRO 1.29, FLUOROCHEM 1.07, GLAXO 0.59, which needs a 63% win rate merely to break even. The defect was that a week qualifying nobody wrote nothing at all, so the page served the 1 August list as though it were current. The attempt is recorded either way now. The gate is NOT loosened: publishing a 0.59 R:R to keep the section busy is the exact trade this screen exists to refuse, and an empty week is a real result.

engine.title: Stop buying strength that has already run
engine.body: The 4H RSI ceiling for longs was 75. Splitting every closed trade by the RSI recorded at entry showed the engine bleeding above 65 and profitable below it. The ceiling is now 65.
engine.note: Holds in both halves of the sample and at every cut point tested (60, 65, 70), so it is not one lucky threshold. The threshold was still chosen from this sample, so treat the size as an upper bound.

engine.title: A break-even stop would not have helped
engine.body: The median losing trade was +1.44R in profit before it reversed, and 59% touched a full +1R first. That looks like an obvious fix: move the stop to entry once price pays 1R. Re-walking every trade bar by bar, with winners subject to the same rule, says otherwise.
engine.note: The first version of this test only altered losers, which guarantees a positive answer. Correcting it reversed the conclusion. Nothing tested cleared one standard error, so no stop rule was adopted.

engine.title: Trades were being closed at prices that never traded
engine.body: The grader had never resolved a single trade — an exception was being swallowed silently — leaving a fallback path that could book an exit at a bar from before the signal existed. Every closed trade was re-graded against bars that actually printed.
evidence: exits corrected to a real price
engine.note: This moved the headline number against me. It is published anyway, because the earlier number was not real. Pre-correction data is kept in the repo rather than deleted.

engine.title: A first target must pay back the risk
engine.body: T1 was whichever structural level sat nearest the entry, with no distance test. One signal shipped a T1 worth 0.19R against its own stop, printed beside an R:R of 2.41 quoted off T2. T1 must now return at least 1R.

book.author: Atul Gawande
book.chapter: Checklists Are Not for Dumb People. They're for Experts.
book.lesson: Surgeon Atul Gawande studied why brilliant surgeons and pilots make elementary errors. The answer: not incompetence but complexity. Modern tasks have too many steps for any brain to hold reliably under pressure. His solution, borrowed from aviation: checklists. A two-minute surgical checklist reduced surgical complications by 36% and deaths by 47% in a global study. The lesson for knowledge work: expertise does not eliminate the need for process discipline. The most error-prone moments are not the hard parts of a task — they're the routine parts where experts assume they can proceed from memory. They can't.
book.key_quote: Checklists are not about distrust of expertise. They are about respecting the limits of human memory under pressure.
book.action: Identify your most error-prone recurring process (month-end close, financial review). Write a checklist for it this week. Use it next time.
crux: Failure in complex work is usually not ignorance. It is ineptitude — knowing what to do and not doing it.
Volume and complexity of knowledge now exceed what any individual can reliably hold in working memory.
Checklists convert known steps into guaranteed steps.
Two failure types: errors of ignorance (we don't know) and errors of ineptitude (we know but slipped). Checklists kill the second.
Good checklists are short — 5 to 9 items, one page, pause points at natural breaks.
Bad checklists are long, vague, and try to spell out every step. They get ignored.
DO-CONFIRM (act, then verify) versus READ-DO (read each line, then act). Pick deliberately.
Checklists must be tested in the real setting. Desk-designed lists fail in the field.
The largest gain is often communication: forcing names, roles, and concerns to be stated aloud.
A five-item surgical checklist cut deaths 47% and complications 36% across eight hospitals.
Experts resist checklists because they feel insulting. That reaction is the reason they are needed.
Discipline is harder than brilliance, and rarer.
learnings: Skill does not protect against the routine slip. Structure does.
The resistance to a checklist is ego, and ego is expensive.
Writing the list down is what converts intention into reliability.
Forcing people to speak up is a safety feature, not politeness.
examples: Boeing's Model 299 crashed in 1935 because pilots forgot one lock. A one-page checklist let the B-17 fly 1.8 million miles without a similar accident.
Johns Hopkins used a five-line central-line checklist and cut infection rates from 11% to zero over a year.
Van Halen's brown-M&M clause was a checklist canary: if the M&Ms were unsorted, the rigging had not been read either.
adapt: Pre-post checklist for Instagram: score the caption, check restricted terms, confirm no financial-advice phrasing. Five items, one screen.
Pre-deploy checklist: type-check, lint, verify which Vercel project the alias actually points at.
Month-end close checklist. Same order every month. Speed comes from the order, not from hurrying.
Pre-trade checklist: regime, stop distance versus ATR, position already open? The 59 duplicate NATGAS rows were an ineptitude error, not an ignorance one.

interview_tech.q: You suspect fraud in a store's cash handling. What is your first move?
interview_tech.a: Do not confront and do not alert. Preserve evidence first — secure the system logs, till data, CCTV and reconciliations before anyone knows there is a question. Then escalate per policy: internal audit, legal, and whoever the fraud policy names, usually the audit committee chair for anything material or involving management. Only then investigate. The most common and most costly mistake is a well-meaning manager asking questions locally, which destroys evidence and tips off the person involved.
interview_tech.who: Any group with an audit committee

interview_tech.q: How would you build the finance case for entering Saudi Arabia?
interview_tech.a: Model it as an option, not a certainty. Entry costs: legal structure and Saudisation obligations under Nitaqat, which drive a materially different payroll cost curve; local content and CITC/ZATCA compliance; e-invoicing (FATOORA) from day one. Revenue: a much larger population than the UAE with different mall economics and a younger consumer. Build the base case on 3–5 stores, not the full ambition, with an explicit go/no-go gate after 24 months and a costed exit. The board decision you want is a staged commitment.

interview_soft.q: Describe a time you had to deliver bad news to senior stakeholders.
interview_soft.a: Lead with the structure you used, because that is the skill. Bad news goes: the number, the cause, the impact, the plan, the ask. No preamble. Deliver it early even when incomplete — 'here is what I know now and what I will know Friday' beats a complete answer a week late. Give a specific example with the actual figure and what you did next. The tell they look for: did you surface it or did someone else find it.

interview_soft.q: Why should we hire you over a candidate with Big Four and listed-company experience?
interview_soft.a: Do not disparage the alternative. Frame the trade: audit teaches you to verify what happened; operating finance teaches you to change what happens next. Then be specific about what you own that they do not — a live multi-country P&L, an ERP implementation you led rather than advised on, and store-level decisions you made and were held to. End with the honest gap and how you would close it. Confidence with a named weakness beats confidence alone.

cfo_field.q: The offer is decided by the non-technical questions.
cfo_field.a: Everyone shortlisted can do the technical work — that is why they were shortlisted. What separates the offer is whether the panel believes you can hold a room, disagree with a CEO without theatre, and be trusted with bad news. Prepare the failure story properly: what you decided, what it cost, what you changed afterwards. A candidate with no failure story reads as someone who has never owned a decision.

cfo_field.q: A forecast that is never wrong is a forecast nobody is using.
cfo_field.a: Track forecast accuracy as a metric in its own right — absolute percentage error by month, by category. Under 5% at group level is good in retail; over 15% and the business has stopped believing you. But an FP&A team that is never wrong is sandbagging, and sandbagging is more expensive than error: it prices in a buffer everyone plans around, and the buffer compounds up the hierarchy.
